units.title: The Endocrine System
units.intro:
**Exocrine** glands have ducts (sweat, saliva). **Endocrine** glands are ductless — hormones go straight into blood and hunt a *target organ*. Compared with nerves: hormones are slower and last longer (growth, metabolism, cycles).

A gland fires when nerves poke it, or when another hormone pokes it (the pituitary is the usual “boss”).

The Endocrine Glands
body: Tap a gland on the figure to see what it secretes.

The main endocrine glands are the **hypothalamus** and **pituitary** (in the head; the pituitary is the "master gland" that controls other glands), the **thyroid** and **parathyroids** (neck), the **thymus** (chest), the **adrenal glands** (on top of the kidneys), the **islets of Langerhans** in the pancreas, and the **gonads** — ovaries and testes.
Endocrine glands are ductless: they release hormones straight into the blood, which carries them to target organs.

cards.title: Before the glands: hormone, target, feedback — the four words you need
body: **Step 1 — two kinds of gland.** An **exocrine gland** (exo = out) pours its juice through a **duct** onto a surface or into a cavity: sweat, saliva, tears, pancreatic juice. An **endocrine gland** (endo = within) has **no duct**: it releases its product straight into the **blood** (or lymph) that flows through it. That is why endocrine glands have a **rich blood supply**.

**Step 2 — the product is a hormone.** “Hormone” means “to urge on”. A hormone is a **chemical messenger**, made in very small (minute) amounts, released in response to a **specific stimulus**, and carried by the blood to the whole body.

**Step 3 — only target cells answer.** Every cell meets the hormone, but only cells with the matching **receptor** respond. These are the **target cells / target organ**. Example: TSH reaches every organ, but only the thyroid has TSH receptors.

**Step 4 — the level is kept steady by feedback.** The brain (hypothalamus) and the pituitary measure the hormone level. When the level is too high they **switch the gland off**; when it is too low they switch it on. This is **negative feedback** — the result works against (negates) the change.

**Step 5 — two ways a gland is told to secrete** (textbook p.2): (i) by **nerve impulses** from the central nervous system (e.g. adrenal medulla), or (ii) by a **hormone from another gland** (e.g. the thyroid obeys TSH from the pituitary).

body: **Insulin is a protein**, so if swallowed it is digested like meat in the stomach and intestine — that is why diabetics **inject** insulin.
**Steroids are lipids**, so they are made in cells rich in smooth ER (adrenal cortex, gonads) and can be given as tablets (e.g. the contraceptive pill).

cards.title: 1.1.1 The pituitary gland — the “master gland”
body: **Where and what:** a small, **bean (pea)-sized** gland hanging by a stalk from the **hypothalamus** at the base of the brain. It is called the **master gland** because its hormones control the activity of almost all the other endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads, breasts).
**Two lobes, two different jobs.** Structurally and functionally the pituitary is two glands joined together:

**Anterior lobe (front)** — **makes and releases six hormones**: growth hormone (GH, somatotropin), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), prolactin (lactogenic hormone), and the two gonadotropins, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH).

**Posterior lobe (back)** — **makes no hormone**. It **stores and releases two** hormones that are **made in the hypothalamus** by neurosecretory cells and passed down nerve fibres in the stalk: **antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also called vasopressin)** and **oxytocin**.

**Who controls the master?** The **hypothalamus**, a small part of the brain below the thalamus. It is the main control centre of the endocrine system: it sends **releasing hormones** through tiny blood vessels to the anterior lobe and **nerve impulses** to the posterior lobe. So the hypothalamus links the **nervous system** to the **endocrine system**.
**Why “tropic”?** A tropic hormone (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) has **another endocrine gland** as its target. GH and prolactin act directly on body tissues.

body: Read top to bottom: the hypothalamus controls the anterior lobe through **blood vessels** (releasing hormones) and the posterior lobe through **nerve fibres** (ADH and oxytocin travel down them).

cards.title: Negative feedback of gonadotropins (Figure 1.2) step by step

steps.text: **Step 1:** the hypothalamus releases **GnRH** (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) into the blood vessels of the stalk.
**Step 2:** GnRH makes the anterior pituitary release **FSH and LH**.
**Step 3:** FSH and LH make the testes or ovaries produce gametes and **sex hormones** (testosterone / oestrogen, progesterone).
**Step 4:** the sex hormones act on target cells (secondary sexual characteristics, uterus, sperm production).
**Step 5 — feedback:** a high level of sex hormone acts back on the hypothalamus and pituitary: **less GnRH, FSH and LH** are released, so sex-hormone production falls back to normal.

cards.title: ADH step by step: how the body saves water
body: **Step 1 — sensing:** neurons in the hypothalamus are sensitive to the water–salt balance of the blood (osmoreceptors).
**Step 2 — too concentrated** (you sweated, ate salty food, did not drink): the hypothalamus signals and **ADH is released** from the posterior lobe.

**Step 3 — action:** in the kidneys ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable, so **more water is reabsorbed** from the filtered plasma back into the blood. Urine becomes **small in volume and concentrated** (dark).
**Step 4 — back to normal:** the blood becomes more dilute, the hypothalamus detects it and **ADH release stops** (negative feedback).
**Step 5 — too dilute** (you drank a lot): almost no ADH → little water reabsorbed → **large volume of dilute urine**.
**Exam link (Review Q8):** **alcohol inhibits ADH release**, so a drinker fails to reabsorb water, produces a lot of dilute urine and becomes dehydrated (headache, thirst next morning).

cards.title: Anterior lobe = “FLAT PG”; posterior = “ADH & OXY live in the back”
body: **FLAT PG** — the six anterior hormones: **F**SH, **L**H, **A**CTH, **T**SH, **P**rolactin, **G**H. (Picture a flat PG-rated film shown at the **front** of the cinema.)
**Posterior = storeroom at the back:** it only keeps **ADH** and **OXY**tocin that the hypothalamus made. Say: “The back room stores what the boss (hypothalamus) made.”
**ADH = Anti-Diuresis = Anti-“lots of urine”** → saves water. **Oxytocin = “Ox-y-quick birth”** → strong push in labour and milk let-down.

cards.title: Exam traps — pituitary
body: **Trap 1:** “The posterior pituitary produces ADH” → **false**: it **stores and releases**; the hypothalamus **produces** it.
**Trap 2:** **Thymosin, insulin, thyroxine** are NOT pituitary hormones (Review Q3 → thymosin).

**Trap 3:** **Diabetes insipidus** is an **ADH (posterior pituitary / hypothalamus)** problem: much dilute urine and thirst, **no glucose** in urine. (Your textbook p.18 mistakenly calls it a pancreas disorder with glucose in urine — that describes **diabetes mellitus**. Learn the correct version.)
**Trap 4:** pituitary dwarf = **normal intelligence**, normal proportions; cretin (thyroid) = **mental retardation**, disproportionate body.

cards.title: Worked example: why is the pituitary called the master gland? (Exercise 1.1 Q4)
cards.problem: Explain why the pituitary is called the “master gland”, and why this name is only partly true.

steps.text: **Step 1 — list what it controls:** TSH → thyroid; ACTH → adrenal cortex; FSH and LH → testes and ovaries; prolactin → breasts; GH → growth of the whole body.
**Step 2 — conclude the first part:** because its hormones switch other endocrine glands on and off, it “masters” them.
**Step 3 — the limit:** the pituitary itself obeys the **hypothalamus** (releasing hormones and nerve fibres) and is switched off by **feedback** from the hormones of its target glands.

cards.answer: It is called the master gland because its tropic hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) control the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads, and GH and prolactin act on the whole body. Strictly, the hypothalamus is the real control centre, so the pituitary is a “master” under the brain’s command.

cards.title: Worked example: Activity 1.2 — the stalk nerves are damaged
cards.problem: All the neuron connections between the hypothalamus and the pituitary are severely damaged. Which pituitary hormones are affected, and which are not?

steps.text: **Step 1 — recall which lobe uses nerves:** ADH and oxytocin are **made in hypothalamic neurons** and travel **down nerve fibres** to the posterior lobe.
**Step 2 — so cutting the nerves stops them:** ADH and oxytocin are no longer released → large volumes of dilute urine (diabetes insipidus) and weak labour/milk let-down.

**Step 3 — the anterior lobe** is controlled through **blood vessels** (releasing hormones), not nerve fibres, and it **makes its own hormones** → GH, TSH, ACTH, prolactin, FSH and LH can still be produced (the textbook answer: “not affected” by nerve damage).

cards.answer: Affected: ADH and oxytocin (posterior lobe). Not affected by the nerve damage: the six anterior-lobe hormones (GH, TSH, ACTH, prolactin, FSH, LH), because they are made in the anterior lobe and controlled through blood vessels.

cards.title: Worked example: urine after drinking two litres of water
cards.problem: A student drinks two litres of water quickly. Describe step by step what happens to ADH and to her urine.

steps.text: **Step 1:** water is absorbed → blood becomes **dilute** (lower salt concentration).
**Step 2:** hypothalamus osmoreceptors detect this → **less ADH** is released from the posterior pituitary.
**Step 3:** collecting ducts become less permeable → **less water reabsorbed**.
**Step 4:** a **large volume of pale, dilute urine** is produced until the blood returns to normal; then ADH rises again to its usual level.

cards.answer: ADH secretion falls, less water is reabsorbed in the kidneys, and she passes a large volume of dilute urine (negative feedback restores the blood concentration).

cards.title: 1.1.2 The thyroid gland — the body’s throttle
body: **Where and what:** a **butterfly-shaped** gland at the **base of the neck in front of the trachea** (windpipe): two lobes joined by a narrow bridge (isthmus). It is the **largest endocrine gland** in the body. Inside, tiny round sacs (follicles) store the hormone.
**Two hormones:** **thyroxine (T4)** and **calcitonin**.

**Thyroxine — needs iodine.** Iodine is an essential part of the thyroxine molecule, so the diet must contain iodine (sea food, **iodised salt**). Chief jobs: (1) controls the body’s **metabolic rate** — how fast cells use oxygen and food to release energy and heat; (2) regulates **growth of bones** and (3) the **development of the brain and nervous system in children**; (4) controls metamorphosis in amphibians (tadpole → frog).

**Calcitonin — lowers blood calcium.** It is secreted when blood calcium **rises**, and it lowers it by promoting **deposition of calcium into bone**. Calcium is needed for nerve conduction, muscle contraction, blood clotting and bone and teeth formation. Its partner (opposite) is **PTH from the parathyroids**, which raises blood calcium.
**What controls the thyroid?** The amount of **iodine** in the body and a **feedback system** involving the hypothalamus and pituitary (TRH → TSH → thyroxine).

cards.title: Negative feedback of thyroxine (Figure 1.5) step by step

steps.text: **Step 1:** the hypothalamus senses a **low thyroxine** level (or cold) and releases **TRH**.
**Step 2:** TRH makes the anterior pituitary release **TSH** into the blood.
**Step 3:** TSH makes the thyroid take up **iodine** and release **thyroxine**.
**Step 4:** thyroxine raises the metabolic rate of target cells.

**Step 5 — feedback:** if the thyroid secretes **too much thyroxine**, the high level signals the hypothalamus and pituitary to release **less TRH and TSH**, so thyroxine secretion **falls**. Too little thyroxine → the brake is released → more TSH.

cards.title: Why a lack of iodine makes the neck swell (goitre) — step by step
body: **Step 1:** no iodine in food → the thyroid **cannot make thyroxine**.
**Step 2:** thyroxine level in blood is **low**, so there is **no negative feedback** on the pituitary.
**Step 3:** the pituitary keeps pouring out **TSH**.
**Step 4:** TSH keeps stimulating the thyroid to **grow** — the gland enlarges and the neck swells: **goitre** (simple or iodine-deficiency goitre, common in mountain areas far from the sea).
**Prevention and treatment:** a balanced diet with **iodised salt**; iodine tablets if needed (textbook p.19).

**Two kinds of goitre:** your textbook (pp.18–20) lists goitre under **over-secretion** (an overactive, enlarged thyroid — hyperthyroid goitre, caused by plasma proteins that over-stimulate the gland). The goitre from **iodine deficiency** comes with **low** thyroxine. In an exam: “goitre = swelling of the thyroid”; “disease caused by lack of iodine = goitre” (Review Part II Q6).

cards.title: Worked example: poor growth in a one-year-old (Activity 1.5 Q2)
cards.problem: Without measuring hormones, how would you tell thyroid deficiency from growth-hormone deficiency as the cause of poor growth in a one-year-old child?

steps.text: **Step 1 — recall what thyroxine does in children:** it controls **brain development** and metabolic rate as well as growth.
**Step 2 — signs of thyroid deficiency (cretinism):** slow mental development, sluggish, large tongue, dry skin, feels cold, **body out of proportion**.
**Step 3 — signs of GH deficiency (pituitary dwarfism):** small but **well-proportioned**, **normal mental development**, normal skin and activity.
**Step 4 — decide:** mental/behavioural development and body proportions separate the two.

cards.answer: A thyroid-deficient child is mentally slow, sluggish, with dry skin, large tongue and disproportionate body (cretinism); a GH-deficient child is small but proportionate with normal intelligence and activity.

cards.title: Worked example: hormone high but signs of deficiency (Review Part I Q1)
cards.problem: A person shows the signs of thyroid hormone deficiency, but has above-average levels of thyroid hormone in the blood. What might the problem be? A. inadequate TSH B. too much TSH C. too few thyroid-hormone receptors in body cells D. too few TSH receptors in thyroid cells

steps.text: **Step 1:** the hormone is **present in plenty**, so the gland and TSH are not the problem (A, B, D would change the hormone level).
**Step 2:** a hormone acts only through its **receptors**. If target cells lack receptors they cannot “hear” it → deficiency signs.
**Step 3:** choose the receptor problem in the **target cells**.

cards.answer: C — the body cells have too few thyroid-hormone receptors, so the hormone cannot act.

cards.title: Worked example: a man takes extra thyroxine tablets
cards.problem: A man takes thyroxine tablets he does not need for several months. Predict what happens to (a) his TSH level, (b) the size of his own thyroid gland, (c) his body weight.

steps.text: **Step 1 — blood thyroxine is high** (from tablets).
**Step 2 — negative feedback:** high thyroxine → hypothalamus and pituitary release **less TRH and TSH**.
**Step 3 — no TSH stimulation** → his own thyroid becomes inactive and **shrinks**.
**Step 4 — high metabolic rate** → more food burned → **weight loss**, sweating, fast heart.

cards.answer: (a) TSH falls; (b) his thyroid shrinks (no TSH stimulation); (c) he loses weight because his metabolic rate is high.

cards.title: 1.1.3 The Parathyroid Glands
body: Parathyroid (para – meaning beside) glands are usually four small, flattened glands which are located behind the thyroid gland.
The parathyroid glands secrete a parathyroid hormone (PTH), or parathormone, that controls the concentration of calcium ions in the blood.
The correct amounts of calcium ions in the bloodstream are necessary for muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, bone and teeth development, blood clotting and other tasks.
When the concentration of calcium ions in the blood decreases, PTH activates bone cells to release calcium and phosphate ions, and stimulates the kidneys to conserve them.

cards.title: 1.1.4 The adrenal glands — the stress (emergency) glands
body: **Where and what:** a pair of small, **yellow** masses of tissue, **one on top of each kidney** (ad = near, renal = kidney). They are called the **stress glands** or the “emergency gland”.
**Two glands in one.** Each adrenal has an outer **cortex** and an inner **medulla**; they differ in structure, in the hormones they make and in how they are controlled.
**Adrenal cortex (outer, bulky part)** — secretes many **steroid** hormones called **corticosteroids (corticoids)**, in three groups:

**a. Glucocorticoids**, mainly **cortisol**: regulate the metabolism of fats, proteins and carbohydrates (raise blood glucose by breaking down fats and proteins), help the body **adapt to long-term stress**, repair damaged tissues, and also affect blood pressure, energy balance and white blood cell production.

**b. Mineralocorticoids**, mainly **aldosterone**: regulate **water and mineral balance**, especially **sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺)**. Secreted when blood Na⁺ is **low** or K⁺ is **high**; makes the kidney tubules **reabsorb (keep) sodium** and **excrete potassium**; water follows the sodium.
**c. Sex steroids**: small amounts of androgens (and oestrogen). The most potent androgen, testosterone, comes mainly from the testes.

**Adrenal medulla (inner part)** — behaves like part of the nervous system: it **receives nerve impulses from the brain** and releases **adrenaline (epinephrine)** and **noradrenaline (norepinephrine)**. Adrenaline is the **“fight or flight”** hormone; noradrenaline mainly **constricts blood vessels** throughout the body.

cards.title: Adrenal gland: cortex and medulla

cards.title: A dog chases you — the adrenal response step by step

steps.text: **Step 1:** your eyes see the danger; the brain sends **nerve impulses** down a nerve to the **adrenal medulla**.
**Step 2:** within seconds the medulla releases **adrenaline** into the blood: heart races, glucose rises, you run.
**Step 3:** if stress lasts (days of worry, illness), the hypothalamus–pituitary send **ACTH** → the **cortex** releases **cortisol**, keeping blood glucose up from fat and protein.
**Step 4:** if you lose a lot of salt and water (sweating, bleeding), the cortex releases **aldosterone** so the kidneys keep Na⁺ and water.

cards.title: Adrenal memory: “Cortex = Salt, Sugar, Sex · Medulla = Moment of danger”
body: **Cortex → 3 S’s:** **S**alt (aldosterone), **S**ugar (cortisol), **S**ex (sex steroids). All are **steroids** — another S.
**Medulla → M for Moment:** works in the moment of danger, switched on by **nerves**, not by the pituitary.
**Addison = Adds nothing** (too little cortex hormone). **Cushing = Cushion** (too much cortisol: round, padded face and body).

cards.title: Worked example: how the adrenals help with stress or fear (Exercise 1.1 Q2)
cards.problem: (a) State the location of the adrenal glands. (b) Explain how they help the body cope with stress or fear.

steps.text: **(a)** One adrenal gland sits on top of each kidney.
**(b) Step 1 — sudden fear:** nerve impulses → medulla → **adrenaline** → faster heart and breathing, glycogen → glucose in the liver, blood to muscles, wider pupils → energy to fight or run.
**Step 2 — long stress:** ACTH → cortex → **cortisol** → blood glucose kept high from fats and proteins, tissue repair.
**Step 3 — loss of salt/water:** **aldosterone** keeps sodium and water, protecting blood pressure.

cards.answer: (a) On top of each kidney. (b) The medulla releases adrenaline for immediate “fight or flight” (heart rate, glucose, blood to muscles); the cortex releases cortisol for long-term stress (raises glucose, repairs tissues) and aldosterone to keep salt and water.

cards.title: Worked example: glucocorticoid — like glucagon or insulin? (Exercise 1.1 Q6)
cards.problem: Does the action of a glucocorticoid (cortisol) more closely resemble that of glucagon or of insulin? Explain.

steps.text: **Step 1 — insulin:** lowers blood glucose (glucose → glycogen, into cells).
**Step 2 — glucagon:** raises blood glucose (glycogen → glucose).
**Step 3 — cortisol:** raises blood glucose by breaking down fats and proteins as an energy source (textbook Table 1.1: “raise blood glucose level”).
**Step 4 — compare:** cortisol and glucagon both **raise** blood glucose.

cards.answer: Glucagon — both raise the blood glucose level (cortisol by breaking down fats and proteins), whereas insulin lowers it.

cards.title: Worked example: nerves to the adrenal medulla are cut (Activity 1.3 Q1)
cards.problem: In an experimental animal the sympathetic nerve fibres to the adrenal medulla are cut. What happens to adrenaline (epinephrine) concentration at rest and during stress?

steps.text: **Step 1:** the medulla releases adrenaline only when **nerve impulses** arrive.
**Step 2 — at rest:** the level is normally low anyway → stays low (little change).
**Step 3 — during stress:** no impulses reach the medulla → **no rise** in adrenaline (only the sympathetic nerves themselves can help with noradrenaline).

cards.answer: At rest the level stays low; during stress adrenaline does not rise, because the medulla is switched on only by nerve impulses.

cards.title: 1.1.5 The pancreas — a double gland
body: **Where and what:** a soft, flattened organ **below the stomach**, in the loop of the duodenum (“pan” = all, “kreas” = flesh). It is both an **exocrine** and an **endocrine** gland.
**Exocrine part (most of the pancreas):** cells make **pancreatic juice** (digestive enzymes) that flows through the **pancreatic duct** into the duodenum.

**Endocrine part:** small groups of cells scattered through the pancreas — the **islets of Langerhans**. Each islet contains **alpha (α) cells**, which secrete **glucagon**, and **beta (β) cells**, which secrete **insulin**. (Delta cells make a third hormone, somatostatin — extra.)
**The islets are glucose sensors.** They constantly monitor the blood glucose level. Normal: about **100 mg of glucose in every 100 cm³ of blood** (textbook p.11).

**Glucose too high** (after a meal) → β-cells release **insulin** → liver (and muscle) cells take up glucose and **convert excess glucose into glycogen**; body cells take in and respire more glucose → level falls.
**Glucose too low** (fasting, exercise) → α-cells release **glucagon** → liver **converts stored glycogen into glucose** and releases it → level rises.
Insulin and glucagon are **antagonistic** hormones: they have opposite effects and together keep the level steady (Figure 1.8).

cards.title: Antagonistic control of blood sugar (Figure 1.8) step by step

steps.text: **High glucose (after a meal):** β-cells sense it and release **insulin**. Liver and muscle take glucose in and store it as **glycogen**; cells respire more → glucose falls back to normal.
**Low glucose (fasting, hard work):** α-cells release **glucagon**. The liver breaks **glycogen → glucose** and releases it into the blood → glucose rises back to normal.
**Negative feedback:** the change itself (glucose level) is what the islets detect — no pituitary hormone is involved.

cards.title: Diabetes mellitus step by step
body: **Step 1 — cause:** the β-cells fail to make insulin (**type 1**, usually starts young; needs insulin injections) or the body cells stop responding to insulin (**type 2**, usually adults, linked to overweight and inactivity; diet, exercise and tablets help).
**Step 2 — glucose stays in the blood:** without insulin, cells cannot take up glucose and the liver cannot store it as glycogen → blood glucose is **abnormally high**.
**Step 3 — glucose in urine:** the kidneys cannot reabsorb so much glucose → glucose appears in the urine (a simple urine test shows it).
**Step 4 — water follows:** glucose in urine carries water with it → **excessive urination** → **intense thirst**.
**Step 5 — energy crisis:** cells are “starving in plenty” → they break down fats and proteins → **weight loss**, tiredness.
**Step 6 — danger:** very high blood glucose can damage brain cells → **coma and possibly death** (textbook p.19). Too much injected insulin causes the opposite danger, **hypoglycaemia**.
**Why a sugary diet is dangerous for a diabetic (Let us discuss p.17):** extra sugar is absorbed into the blood, but without insulin it cannot be stored or used, so blood glucose rises even higher.

body: **β-cells → insulin → Builds glycogen** (stores glucose). **α-cells → glucagon → takes glucose Away from the store.**
**Insulin puts glucose IN** (into cells, into the glycogen store). **GlucaGON**: “the glucose is GONE — bring it back!”
**Glycogen vs glucagon:** glycogen is the **store** (a carbohydrate, like a **gen**erator in the liver); glucagon is the **hormone** (it is **gone** after acting).

cards.title: Worked example: a diabetic breaks a leg (Exercise 1.2 Q3)
cards.problem: A person with diabetes mellitus breaks a leg. Would you advise an increase or a decrease in the insulin dose? Explain.

steps.text: **Step 1 — injury is stress:** stress raises **adrenaline** and **cortisol**.
**Step 2 — both raise blood glucose** (glycogen → glucose; fats and proteins used).
**Step 3 — a diabetic cannot make extra insulin** to bring the glucose down.
**Step 4 — so the dose usually needs to go up** (under a doctor’s supervision, with blood glucose checked often).

cards.answer: Increase it (with medical advice): the stress of injury releases adrenaline and cortisol, which raise blood glucose, and the diabetic cannot produce extra insulin.

cards.title: Worked example: reading blood glucose after a meal
cards.problem: A student’s blood glucose is 100 mg/100 cm³ before breakfast, 150 mg/100 cm³ 45 minutes after eating injera with honey, and 100 mg/100 cm³ again after 2½ hours. Explain each change and name the hormone involved.

steps.text: **Step 1 — rise (100 → 150):** digested carbohydrate is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood.
**Step 2 — detection:** β-cells of the islets sense the high level and release **insulin**.
**Step 3 — fall (150 → 100):** insulin makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as **glycogen**; cells respire more.
**Step 4 — later, between meals:** if it drops below normal, α-cells release **glucagon** to release glucose from glycogen.

cards.answer: The rise is absorption of digested food; insulin from β-cells brings it back to about 100 mg/100 cm³ by glucose uptake and glycogen formation (negative feedback); glucagon would prevent a later fall.

cards.title: Worked example: urine changes (Review Part IV Q3b)
cards.problem: How does hyposecretion of insulin affect the quantity and composition of urine?

steps.text: **Step 1:** too little insulin → blood glucose too high.
**Step 2:** the kidney tubules cannot reabsorb all the filtered glucose → **glucose in the urine**.
**Step 3:** glucose holds water in the tubules (osmosis) → **larger volume** of urine.

cards.answer: Urine becomes larger in volume and contains glucose.

cards.title: 1.1.6 The sex glands (gonads) — hormones and gametes
body: **What:** the **testes** (male) and **ovaries** (female) are the primary reproductive organs (**gonads**). They do two jobs: they produce **gametes** (sperm, ova) and secrete **sex hormones** that create the male or female characteristics.

**Testes:** two oval glands in the scrotum. Between the sperm-forming tubules lie **Leydig (interstitial) cells** — the endocrine tissue. When stimulated by **LH** from the pituitary, Leydig cells release **androgens**, mainly **testosterone**, into the blood. **FSH** stimulates the seminiferous tubules to produce **sperm** (testosterone is needed too).
**When it starts:** at the beginning of adolescence (**puberty**), when the hypothalamus increases GnRH and so FSH and LH.

**Testosterone causes male secondary sexual characteristics:** deeper voice, body and facial hair (beard), increased muscle, broader chest and shoulders, growth of the penis and testes, sex drive and sperm production.

**Ovaries:** two almond-shaped glands beside the uterus. Under **FSH** a follicle grows and its cells make **oestrogen**; after ovulation, under **LH**, the empty follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which makes **progesterone** (and some oestrogen).

**Oestrogen causes female secondary sexual characteristics** — breast enlargement, broadening of the hips, pubic and armpit hair — and **rebuilds the uterine lining** each month. **Progesterone** **thickens and maintains** the uterine lining for a possible pregnancy and keeps it during pregnancy.

cards.title: Worked example: testes removed before puberty
cards.problem: A boy’s testes are removed before puberty because of disease. Predict (a) his secondary sexual characteristics, (b) his blood LH level. Explain.

steps.text: **Step 1:** testes = source of testosterone (Leydig cells).
**Step 2:** no testosterone → voice stays high, little beard or body hair, less muscle; no sperm.
**Step 3 — feedback:** testosterone normally switches GnRH and LH **down**. With no testosterone, the brake is gone → **LH (and FSH) rise** to high levels.

cards.answer: (a) Male secondary characteristics do not develop (high voice, little facial hair, small muscles) and he is infertile. (b) LH rises, because there is no testosterone to give negative feedback.

cards.title: Worked example: why athletes who abuse steroids can become infertile
cards.problem: Some athletes inject large doses of testosterone-like steroids. Explain why their own testes may shrink and sperm production fall.

steps.text: **Step 1:** the injected steroid raises the androgen level in blood.
**Step 2 — negative feedback:** the hypothalamus and pituitary sense a high level → **less GnRH, FSH and LH**.
**Step 3:** without LH, Leydig cells stop working; without FSH, sperm production falls → testes shrink.

cards.answer: High steroid levels switch off GnRH, FSH and LH by negative feedback, so the testes are no longer stimulated: they shrink and make few sperm.

cards.title: 1.1.7 The thymus gland — school for T cells
body: **Where:** in the central chest cavity, **behind the breastbone (sternum), below the thyroid and above the heart**.

**Changes with age:** relatively **large in newborns and children**, it **shrinks sharply after puberty**. In adults it gradually degenerates until it almost disappears and becomes filled with fibrous and fatty connective tissue. So the thymus is **functional mainly in childhood**.
**Hormone:** **thymosin** (a group of small peptides).

**Function:** thymosin stimulates the production and maturation of white blood cells called **T cells (T lymphocytes)**, which defend the body against pathogens (germs). Young lymphocytes from the bone marrow come to the thymus, **multiply, differentiate and mature** there, then leave to guard the body for life.

**Why it matters:** T cells direct the immune response and kill infected cells. The HIV virus attacks one kind of T cell (helper T cells), which is why AIDS weakens immunity. A child born without a working thymus has very few T cells and suffers repeated infections.
**Is it under the pituitary?** No well-known pituitary control: its activity is mainly set by **age** (large in childhood, shrinks after puberty — sex hormones speed the shrinking).

cards.title: Worked example: thymus removed at birth vs in adulthood
cards.problem: In experiments, removing the thymus from newborn mice causes very weak immunity, but removing it from adult mice has little effect. Explain.

steps.text: **Step 1:** the thymus (thymosin) trains T cells mainly **early in life**.
**Step 2 — newborn:** no thymus → T cells never mature → the immune system cannot fight infections.
**Step 3 — adult:** most T cells have already matured and live on in blood and lymph nodes → removal now changes little.

cards.answer: In newborns the thymus is needed to produce mature T cells; in adults the T-cell population has already been made, so the shrinking (or removed) thymus is no longer essential.

cards.title: Disorders of the endocrine glands
body: **Too little growth hormone** in childhood → dwarfism; **too much** → gigantism. **Lack of iodine** → goitre. **Too little insulin** (or cells not responding) → **diabetes mellitus (high blood glucose). **Too much thyroxine** → overactive thyroid (fast heartbeat, weight loss); **too little** in children → stunted growth and slow mental development.

cards.title: Step by step: Malfunctioning of the endocrine glands
body: **Step 1:** Each gland can produce too much (hyper-) or too little (hypo-) hormone, and either one disturbs the body.
**Step 2:** Pituitary – growth hormone: too little in childhood → dwarfism; too much in childhood → gigantism; too much in adults → acromegaly (enlarged hands, feet, jaw).
**Step 3:** Thyroid – thyroxine: too little → goitre (with iodine shortage), tiredness, weight gain, and cretinism in children; too much → hyperthyroidism (fast heartbeat, weight loss, bulging eyes).
**Step 4:** Pancreas – insulin: too little or cells not responding → diabetes mellitus (high blood sugar, sugar in urine, thirst, frequent urination).
**Step 5:** Adrenal glands: too little cortisol/aldosterone → Addison's disease; too much cortisol → Cushing's syndrome.

**Example:** A person living far from the sea with little iodine in the diet develops a swelling in the neck. Iodine is needed to make thyroxine; the thyroid enlarges trying to make more → goitre. Prevention: iodized salt.

tips.text: In addition to the nervous system, endocrine system is the system for coordination in animals.
The human body contains both exocrine glands and endocrine glands.
Sweat and salivary glands are examples of exocrine glands.
Endocrine glands are called ductless glands.
Examples include the pancreas; and the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal and thymus glands.

Endocrine glands secrete hormones, which are chemical messengers that are released directly into the bloodstream. They are transported over long distances and alter metabolic activities in target cells.
The production of hormones from ductless glands is, however, either directly or indirectly influenced by the nervous system.
The hypothalamus is the major integrating link between the nervous and endocrine systems, by regulating the activity of the pituitary gland.
Hormones play an important role in regulating growth and development in sexual reproduction and in the proper functioning of cells.

questions.q: A group of Grade 11 students in Asmara are classifying the glands of the human body according to how their secretions leave the gland. Which ONE of the following structures is classified as an endocrine gland?

options.D: Digestive gland opening into the small intestine

why: **Recall the defining structural feature.** The unit defines endocrine glands as entirely ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream or surrounding interstitial fluid, using a rich capillary network rather than a duct.

**Recall the defining feature of exocrine glands.** Exocrine glands synthesize secretions that are channelled through anatomical ducts directly to an epithelial surface. Sweat glands, salivary glands and digestive organs are named in the unit as exocrine examples.

**Test each option in turn.** B (sweat gland) and C (salivary gland) deliver their secretions through ducts onto the skin and into the mouth respectively, and D (digestive gland) delivers digestive secretion through a duct into the intestinal lumen; all three are therefore exocrine. The thyroid gland has no duct and releases its hormones, such as thyroxine, into the blood.
**Conclude.** Only the thyroid gland is ductless and blood-borne in its secretion, so it is the only endocrine structure listed.

**Conclude.** Only the salivary gland uses a duct, so it is the exocrine gland required.

**Apply the criteria to the observation.** No duct is present, so the secretion cannot be channelled to an epithelial surface; a very rich capillary network is exactly the feature the unit describes in endocrine glands.
**Conclude.** The gland is endocrine and its secretion consists of hormones released into the blood for systemic transport.

questions.q: A patient in Asmara has a blood sample analysed after a meal and again after an overnight fast. Complete the following paragraph by supplying the missing terms. After a meal, the beta cells of the pancreatic islets release (1) ______, which facilitates glucose transport into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue and promotes the storage of glucose as glycogen, a process called (2) ______. During fasting, the alpha cells release (3) ______, which acts on liver tissue to raise blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and (4) ______, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.
why: **Identify the postprandial hormone and its source.** The unit states that beta cells of the islets of Langerhans produce insulin, which facilitates glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissues during postprandial states and lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake and glycogenesis.
**Name the storage process.** The conversion of absorbed glucose into stored glycogen is termed glycogenesis, so blank (2) is glycogenesis.
**Identify the fasting hormone.** Alpha cells of the same islets synthesize and secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting, acting principally on liver tissue.

**Name the second hepatic route to glucose.** Besides breaking glycogen down (glycogenolysis), glucagon stimulates gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, which fills blank (4).
**State the completed paragraph.** (1) insulin, (2) glycogenesis, (3) glucagon, (4) gluconeogenesis.

**Fill the third blank.** The catecholamine named together with norepinephrine is epinephrine (adrenaline), which stimulates rapid flight-or-fight sympathetic adaptations in the heart, blood vessels and liver.

questions.q: A clinical laboratory in Asmara measures the effect of two pancreatic hormones on isolated liver hepatocytes. Explain how insulin and glucagon exert opposing effects on blood glucose concentration, and state the two processes by which glucagon raises blood glucose.
questions.answer: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake into muscle, adipose tissue and liver and by promoting glycogenesis; glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in liver tissue, making the two hormones antagonistic.
why: **State the source and trigger of each hormone.** Within the islets of Langerhans, beta cells secrete insulin during postprandial (fed) states, while alpha cells secrete glucagon during fasting, so the two hormones are released under opposite physiological conditions.

**Describe the action of insulin on hepatocytes.** Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake of glucose and by promoting glycogenesis, that is, the conversion of glucose into stored glycogen in the liver; it also facilitates glucose transport into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

**Describe the action of glucagon on hepatocytes.** Glucagon acts on liver tissue to raise blood glucose. It stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of stored glycogen back into glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.

**Explain why the pair is described as antagonistic.** Because insulin drives glucose out of the blood into storage while glucagon mobilises glucose from storage into the blood, the two hormones produce opposite net movements of glucose and therefore hold blood glucose within its narrow physiological range.

**Summarise the answer.** Insulin promotes cellular glucose uptake and glycogenesis (lowering blood glucose); glucagon promotes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver (raising blood glucose). The two processes by which glucagon raises blood glucose are glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: A student in Keren writes that glucagon and insulin are secreted by the same cells of the pancreatic islets. Correct this statement and explain how the two hormones together maintain glucose homeostasis.
questions.answer: The statement is wrong: glucagon is secreted by the alpha cells and insulin by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans. Together they maintain homeostasis because insulin lowers blood glucose during postprandial states (cellular uptake and glycogenesis), while glucagon raises it during fasting (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis).
why: **Correct the cell assignment.** The unit states that alpha cells synthesize and secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting, while beta cells produce insulin to facilitate glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissues during postprandial states, so two distinct cell populations are involved.
**State the glucose-lowering arm.** Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake of glucose and by promoting glycogenesis, the storage of glucose as glycogen.
**State the glucose-raising arm.** Glucagon acts on liver tissue, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to release glucose into the blood during fasting.

**Explain the homeostatic outcome.** Because the two hormones are released in opposite nutritional states and drive glucose in opposite directions, their balance keeps blood glucose within tight physiological bounds.

**List the two processes.** In the liver glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of glycogen to glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, both of which raise blood glucose.

questions.q:
A 50 kg woman in Asmara is diagnosed with myxoedema and is prescribed thyroxine replacement at a dose of 3.4 micrograms per kilogram of body mass, given once daily. Each 200-microgram tablet costs 0.40 Nakfa.
(a) Calculate her daily thyroxine dose in micrograms.
(b) Express this daily dose in milligrams.
(c) Calculate the total cost in Nakfa of her thyroxine supply for 30 days.
(d) State the endocrine reason why she must take thyroxine, and explain what will happen to her blood TSH level while the treatment is adequate.
questions.answer: (a) 170 micrograms per day; (b) 0.17 milligram per day; (c) 2.04 Nakfa for a 30-day supply; (d) the thyroxine must be supplied because of hyposecretion of thyroxine (myxoedema), and once the dose restores normal thyroxine the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary reduces the blood TSH level back towards normal.
why: **Identify the given data and the relation needed.** Body mass = 50 kg; dose = 3.4 micrograms per kg per day; tablet content = 200 micrograms; tablet cost = 0.40 Nakfa; duration = 30 days. The daily dose equals the dose per kilogram multiplied by body mass. The unit notes that hormones act in minute quantities measured in micrograms or picograms, so microgram units are appropriate here.
**Calculate the daily dose in micrograms.** Daily dose = 3.4 micrograms per kg x 50 kg = 170 micrograms per day.
**Convert micrograms to milligrams.** Since 1 milligram = 1000 micrograms, divide by 1000: 170 micrograms per day / 1000 = 0.17 milligram per day.

**Calculate the 30-day supply and its cost.** Total mass required = 170 micrograms per day x 30 days = 5100 micrograms = 5.1 milligrams. Cost = 5.1 milligrams x 0.40 Nakfa per milligram = 2.04 Nakfa for the 30-day supply.

**Give the endocrine explanation.** Myxoedema is caused by hyposecretion of thyroxine in an adult, and because thyroxine is the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate, the missing hormone must be supplied from outside. Thyroxine normally exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary; when the replacement dose restores a normal circulating thyroxine concentration, that feedback is re-established and the pituitary stops over-secreting TSH, so blood TSH falls back towards normal.

**State the final results.** (a) 170 micrograms per day; (b) 0.17 milligram per day; (c) 2.04 Nakfa for 30 days; (d) thyroxine replacement is required because the gland hyposecretes the hormone, and adequate treatment suppresses the previously elevated blood TSH back to normal through negative feedback.

**Cost the 60-day supply.** Total mass = 150 micrograms per day x 60 days = 9000 micrograms = 9.0 milligrams. Cost = 9.0 milligrams x 0.50 Nakfa per milligram = 4.50 Nakfa.

A 40 kg woman with adult thyroxine hyposecretion receives a total daily thyroxine dose of 136 micrograms from 200-microgram tablets costing 0.40 Nakfa each.
(a) Calculate the dose per kilogram of body mass in micrograms per kg.
(b) Calculate how many whole tablets she must take each day to meet this dose without exceeding it.
(c) Calculate the cost of a 30-day supply based on the tablets actually taken.
questions.answer: (a) 3.4 micrograms per kg; (b) she must take 1 whole tablet per day, providing 200 micrograms, since no whole number of tablets supplies 136 micrograms exactly; (c) 12.00 Nakfa for 30 days.
why: **Find the dose per kilogram.** Dose per kg = total daily dose / body mass = 136 micrograms / 40 kg = 3.4 micrograms per kg.

**Test whole-tablet amounts.** One tablet provides 200 micrograms, which exceeds 136 micrograms by 64 micrograms, so it is the smallest whole-tablet dose that covers the requirement and is the practical choice; any smaller whole number of tablets gives zero micrograms.
**Cost the 30-day supply.** Cost = 1 tablet per day x 0.40 Nakfa per tablet x 30 days = 12.00 Nakfa.

questions.q:
A 70 kg fisherman from Massawa is diagnosed with hyperthyroidism caused by Graves' disease, and his basal metabolic rate is measured at 168 percent of the value expected for a healthy man of his age and body mass. His expected normal basal metabolic rate is 6800 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy in kJ per day that his body expends above the normal value.
(c) Express this excess as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Explain the endocrine basis of this raised metabolic rate and name the gland and the hormone responsible.
questions.answer: (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day of excess expenditure; (c) 68 percent above the normal basal metabolic rate; (d) the thyroid gland is hypersecreting thyroxine, and because thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, energy expenditure rises far above normal.
why: **Identify the given data and the principle.** Normal basal metabolic rate = 6800 kJ per day; measured rate = 168 percent of normal. Thyroxine is described in the unit as the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate, and hyperthyroidism accelerates metabolic rate to pathological levels.
**Calculate the actual basal metabolic rate.** Actual rate = 1.68 x 6800 kJ per day = 11,424 kJ per day.
**Calculate the excess expenditure.** Excess = 11,424 kJ per day - 6800 kJ per day = 4624 kJ per day.

**Express the excess as a percentage.** Percentage excess = (4624 / 6800) x 100 percent = 0.68 x 100 percent = 68 percent, which agrees with the measured value being 68 percent above the normal 100 percent.

**Explain the endocrine mechanism.** The gland responsible is the thyroid gland, which is hypersecreting thyroxine. Thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, so an excess of thyroxine raises oxygen and fuel consumption above normal. This explains the unit's clinical picture of hyperthyroidism: rapid weight loss despite eating, heat intolerance, hyperactive reflexes and anxiety, together with chronic strain on the cardiovascular system from elevated heart rate and blood pressure.

**State the final results.** (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day in excess; (c) 68 percent above normal; (d) hypersecretion of thyroxine by the thyroid gland elevates the basal metabolic rate of most somatic cells.

questions.q:
A 55 kg woman in Asmara with adult thyroxine hyposecretion has a basal metabolic rate measured at 82 percent of the value expected for a healthy woman of her age and body mass. Her expected normal rate is 5400 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate her actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the energy deficit in kJ per day relative to the normal value.
(c) Express this deficit as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Name the hormone that is deficient and explain why this reduces her basal metabolic rate.
questions.answer: (a) 4428 kJ per day; (b) 972 kJ per day below normal; (c) 18 percent below normal; (d) thyroxine is deficient, and since thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, its shortage lowers metabolism, matching the sluggish metabolism, weight gain and cold sensitivity of myxoedema.
why: **Convert the percentage to a multiplier.** A rate at 82 percent of normal corresponds to a multiplying factor of 0.82 applied to the normal value of 5400 kJ per day.
**Calculate the actual rate.** 0.82 x 5400 kJ per day = 4428 kJ per day.
**Calculate the deficit.** Deficit = 5400 kJ per day - 4428 kJ per day = 972 kJ per day.
**Express the deficit as a percentage.** (972 / 5400) x 100 percent = 18 percent, consistent with 100 percent - 82 percent = 18 percent.

**Explain the endocrine cause.** The deficient hormone is thyroxine, the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate. With less thyroxine acting on most somatic cells, heat production and metabolic rate fall, producing the low metabolic rate, weight gain and cold sensitivity characteristic of myxoedema.

questions.q:
A 16-year-old boy in Keren with a pituitary tumour has a basal metabolic rate measured at 120 percent of the normal value for his age and body mass, his normal rate being 6000 kJ per day. The tumour is hypersecreting Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy expended per day.
(c) Express the excess as a percentage of the normal rate.
(d) Explain the full chain of events from the pituitary tumour to the raised metabolic rate.
questions.answer: (a) 7200 kJ per day; (b) 1200 kJ per day in excess; (c) 20 percent above normal; (d) excess TSH from the tumour over-stimulates the thyroid gland, which synthesizes and releases excess thyroxine; thyroxine then acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, raising energy expenditure by 20 percent.
why: **Calculate the actual rate.** 1.20 x 6000 kJ per day = 7200 kJ per day.
**Calculate the excess.** Excess = 7200 kJ per day - 6000 kJ per day = 1200 kJ per day.
**Express the excess as a percentage.** (1200 / 6000) x 100 percent = 20 percent, consistent with 120 percent - 100 percent = 20 percent.

**Trace the hormonal chain.** TSH has the thyroid gland as its principal target tissue and stimulates the synthesis and release of thyroxine, so a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour drives thyroxine secretion upward.

**Link thyroxine to metabolism.** Thyroxine's target is most somatic cells, where it elevates the basal metabolic rate and regulates heat production; the excess hormone therefore accounts for the measured 20 percent rise in energy expenditure.

questions.answer: When blood glucose rises above normal, β-cells release insulin, which makes the liver and muscles take up glucose and convert it into glycogen, and cells use more glucose, so the level falls.
